L0@P0: SPECTROMETER-DRIVEN SPECTRAL PARTITIONING FOR
L1@P0: HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE CLASSIFICATION
L2@P0: Jun Li1, Yi Liu2, Antonio Plaza2, Peijun Du3 and Mahdi Khodadadzadeh2
L3@P0: 1School of Geography and Planning, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, P. R. China.
L4@P0: 2Hyperspectral Computing Laboratory, Department of Technology of Computers and Communications,
L5@P0: Escuela Polit´ecnica, University of Extremadura, C´aceres, E-10071, Spain.
L6@P0: 3Key Laboratory for Satellite Mapping Technology and Applications of State Administration
L7@P0: of Surveying, Mapping, and Geoinformation of China, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210023, China.
L8@P0: ABSTRACT
L9@P0: Classification is an important and widely used technique for
L10@P0: remotely sensed hyperspectral data interpretation. Although most
L11@P0: techniques developed for classification assume that the spectral signatures provided by an imaging spectrometer can be interpreted as
L12@P0: a unique and continuous signal, in practice this signal may be obtained after the combined individual responses from several different
L13@P0: spectrometers. For instance, the Airborne Visible Infra-Red Imaging
L14@P0: Spectrometer (AVIRIS) system is in fact formed by four different
L15@P0: spectrometers, covering the nominal spectral ranges of 400-700 nm,
L16@P0: 700-1300 nm, 1300-1900 nm, and 1900–2500 nm, respectively. In
L17@P0: this work, we propose a new classification strategy which takes into
L18@P0: account the physical design of the imaging spectrometer system for
L19@P0: partitioning the spectral bands collected by each spectrometer, and
L20@P0: resampling them into different groups or partitions. The final classification result is obtained as a combination of the results obtained
L21@P0: from each individual partition. This concept is illustrated in this
L22@P0: work using AVIRIS data, and our experimental results indicate that
L23@P0: the proposed strategy provides advantages in terms of classification accuracy, in particular, when very limited training samples are
L24@P0: available.
L25@P0: Index Terms— Spectrometer-driven classification, partitioning,
L26@P0: clustering, AVIRIS.
L27@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L28@P0: In the last two decades, imaging spectroscopy (also called hyperspectral remote sensing) has experienced significant developments
L29@P0: [1]. Currently, many sensors onboard airborne and spaceborne platforms are available, and these instruments keep collecting data from
L30@P0: different locations over the Earth [2]. Hyperspectral image classification has been a very important topic of research for interpreting
L31@P0: hyperspectral data [3], in which the main challenges have been given
L32@P0: by the high dimensionality of the data and the limited number of
L33@P0: training samples generally available [4]. A main assumption of most
L34@P0: classification techniques is that the spectral signatures provided by
L35@P0: an imaging spectrometer system for a given pixel can be considered
L36@P0: as a unique and continuous signal.
L37@P0: However, in practice this signal may be obtained after the combined individual responses from several different spectrometers.
L38@P0: For instance, the Airborne Visible Infra-Red Imaging Spectrometer
L39@P0: (AVIRIS) system [5] is in fact formed by four different spectrometers, covering the nominal spectral ranges of 400-700 nm, 700-1300
L40@P0: nm, 1300-1900 nm, and 1900–2500 nm, respectively. These four
L41@P0: spectrometers, called A, B, C and D respectively, have different
L42@P0: characteristics. For instance, in the D spectrometer a carefully specified linear variable blocking filter is used to limit the wavelengths
L43@P0: of light for each element in the detector array. This specialized filter
L44@P0: reduces the noise arising from photons emitted by the spectrometer
L45@P0: in the 1900-2500 nm spectral range. For the A spectrometer, a
L46@P0: 32-element silicon detector array with a blue enhanced response is
L47@P0: used. The B, C and D spectrometers each have 64-element arrays
L48@P0: instead.
L49@P0: Given the fact that different spectrometers have different characteristics, our speculation in this work is that the conventional interpretation that the spectral signatures can be interpreted as unique
L50@P0: and distinct signals may not hold in all cases, and that the use of a
L51@P0: spectrometer-driven partitioning prior to classification may lead to
L52@P0: improved hyperspectral data interpretation results. Specifically, in
L53@P0: this work we propose a new spectrometer-driven classification strategy that considers the differences between the individual spectrometers in the classification step. An important consideration of our
L54@P0: approach is that, as the dimensionality of each spectrometer signal
L55@P0: is much smaller than the whole spectral signal, it allows for the design of a classification system that is efficient in scenarios in which
L56@P0: limited training samples are available a priori. Here we illustrate the
L57@P0: concept using AVIRIS data. In order to handle the existing correlation between spectral bands, we use a band partitioning approach
L58@P0: driven by the four different spectrometers of AVIRIS, as the hyperspectral bands captured by each of them exhibit similar characteristics.
L59@P0: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In section
L60@P0: 2, we first introduce the proposed spectrometer-driven spectral partitioning strategy. Then, we present our classification system based
L61@P0: on the recently developed subspace-based multinomial logistic regression (MLRsub), an efficient technique able to deal with very
L62@P0: limited training samples [6]. Experimental results with AVIRIS data
L63@P0: are given in section 3. Finally, section 4 concludes this work with
L64@P0: some remarks.
L65@P0: 2. SPECTROMETER-DRIVEN PARTITIONING AND
L66@P0: HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE CLASSIFICATION

L68@P0: of AVIRIS hyperspectral data based on the MLRsub classifier. In
L69@P0: the spectrometer subsystem of AVIRIS, light from each of the optical fibers enters a different spectrometer covering a portion of the

L85@P1: 2.1. Spectrometer-Driven Spectral Partitioning
L86@P1: In this subsection we describe the spectrometer-driven spectral partitioning strategy and use the AVIRIS Indian Pines data for illustrative
L87@P1: purposes. Since in this case the spectral vectors are collected by four
L88@P1: spectrometers, the band continuity for each spectrometer is expected
L89@P1: to be quite high. Fig. 2 shows the spectral clustering results obtained
L90@P1: from the adaptive affinity propagation (AAP) approach [7], which
L91@P1: uses the coefficient of correlation as the measurement of similarity.
L92@P1: Fig. 2 illustrates that there are high spectral similarities among continuous bands collected by each of the four spectrometers. Based
L93@P1: on this observation, in this work we perform band partitioning based
L94@P1: on the four spectrometers to resample the spectral bands to different groups (or partitions), such as to exploit the spectral information
L95@P1: by reducing the spectral similarities and increasing the partition distance.
L96@P1: The proposed spectrometer-based spectral partitioning approach
L97@P1: is different from conventional spectral clustering approaches, which
L98@P1: generally considers the spectral signatures as a whole. Therefore,
L99@P1: based on the observed spectral correlations, we resample the bands
L100@P1: into different partitions for each spectrometer. In this study, after
L101@P1: resampling, we obtained a total of five partitions, each with 42 spectral bands. Now each pixel in the original hyperspectral image can
L102@P1: be resampled by taking one spectral band from each one of the five
L103@P1: partitions, so that we can obtain five different (subsampled) representations of the original pixel. In order to illustrate this concept,
L104@P1: Fig. 3(a) shows the spectral signature of pixel at spatial location
L105@P1: (100,100) in the the original AVIRIS Indian Pines data, while Fig.

L177@P2: 3. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
L178@P2: This section describes our experimental results with the AVIRIS Indian Pines scene in Fig. 1. As mentioned in the previous section, after the spectral partitioning and resampling we obtain five partitions,
L179@P2: each with 42 spectral bands. In order to analyze the impact of our
L180@P2: spectrometer-driven partitioning framework on the classification of
L181@P2: the scene, we first analyze the performance of the method as a function of the dimensionality of the estimated subspace by the MLRsub
L182@P2: technique. Then, we analyze the sensitivity of the MLRsub to the
L183@P2: number of training samples, thus addressing the two main issues in
L184@P2: supervised classification of hyperspectral data (dimensionality and
L185@P2: limited training samples). In all cases, we set the parameter β (which
L186@P2: controls the degree of smoothness obtained after applying the MRF
L187@P2: to the classification result obtained by the MLRsub) to β = 2, according to our previous studies [6], in which it was shown that appropriate results could be obtained with β in the range [0.5,4].
L188@P2: 3.1. Impact of the Dimensionality of the Estimated Subspace
L189@P2: In this experiment, 10% of the 10366 pixels available in the ground
L190@P2: truth image in Fig. 1(b) are used for training, while the remaining
L191@P2: samples are used for testing. Fig. 4 shows the overall classification
L192@P2: accuracies (OA) as a function of the dimensionality of the subspace,
L193@P2: for both the original hyperspectral image [see Fig. 1(a)] and for the
L194@P2: five partitions [see Fig. 1(b)]. It is remarkable that the results obtained for each partition are very close to the results obtained using
L195@P2: the original image with all the spectral bands. Another important
L196@P2: observation is that, for all the partitions, the optimal dimensionality
L197@P2: was achieved in the interval [10, 15], as it was also the case for the
L198@P2: original image. This means that working in the partition domain allows further possibilities to determine the optimal subspace dimensionality without losing accuracy in the estimation with regards to
L199@P2: the case in which the original hyperspectral image was used. Since
L200@P2: the estimation of the dimensionality of the subspace is an important
L201@P2: aspect for the MLRsub algorithm, we can conclude that the algorithm performs similarly from this viewpoint in the original and in
L202@P2: the partitioned domain.

L230@P2: 3.2. Impact of the Number of Training Samples
L231@P2: In this experiment we evaluate the impact of the number of available training samples in the proposed spectrometer-driven partitioning approach, as compared to the case in which the full spectral information is used. For simplicity, we analyze the cases in which the
L232@P2: dimensionality of the subspace used for the MLRsub classifier is 11
L233@P2: and 13 (the two best cases in Fig. 4. For that purpose, Fig. 5(a)
L234@P2: shows the OAs (as a function of the number of training samples used
L235@P2: per class) obtained when applying the MLRsub with and without
L236@P2: the proposed partitioning strategy to the AVIRIS Indian Pines scene,
L237@P2: considering that the dimensionality of the subspace is 11. Similarly,
L238@P2: Fig. 5(b) shows the OAs (as a function of the number of training
L239@P2: samples used per class) obtained when applying the MLRsub with
L240@P2: and without the proposed partitioning strategy to the AVIRIS Indian
L241@P2: Pines scene, considering that the dimensionality of the subspace is
L242@P2: now 13. The color areas around each plot in Fig. 5 represent the
L243@P2: standard deviation.
L244@P2: Several conclusions can be obtained from Fig. 5. First and
L245@P2: foremost, the proposed approach with spectral partitioning outperforms the classic MLRsub configuration when limited training samples are available. For instance, the proposed approach obtained an
L246@P2: OA greater than 85% by using only 20 labeled samples per class,
L247@P2: increasing significantly the OA obtained by the original strategy in
L248@P2: the same conditions. Furthermore, it is remarkable that the standard
L249@P2: deviations obtained by the proposed partitioning-based approach are
L250@P2: significantly smaller than those achieved by the MLRsub with the
L251@P2: original hyperspectral image. Finally it is also noticeable that, after a given number of training samples (i.e., 60 samples per class in
L252@P2: our experiment), the results obtained with the full original image are
L253@P2: better than those obtained using th proposed partitioning approach.
L254@P2: This is due to the fact that the dimensionality of the partitions and
L255@P2: the class boundaries are well-defined after a sufficient set of training
L256@P2: samples are available.
L257@P2: Finally, Fig. 6 shows the obtained classification maps for the
L258@P2: AVIRIS Indian Pines by using 20 labeled samples per class under an
L259@P2: optimal setting of dimensionality of the subspace. In this particular case, the proposed approach obtained an OA of 87.83% which is
L260@P2: about 20% higher than the OA obtained after applying the MLRsub
L261@P2: (plus the MRF regularization) to the full original hyperspectral image. We can therefore conclude that the proposed spectrometerdriven partitioning approach can provide good classification results

L268@P3: 4. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE LINES
L269@P3: In this work, we have developed a new spectrometer-driven based
L270@P3: technique for hyperspectral image partitioning and classification.
L271@P3: The proposed approach takes into account the physical design of
L272@P3: the imaging spectrometer system for partitioning the spectral bands
L273@P3: collected by each spectrometer, and resampling them into different
L274@P3: groups or partitions. Instead of considering the spectral signatures as
L275@P3: unique continuous signals, here we consider each spectral signature
L276@P3: as a signal that is contributed from different instrument sources, and
L277@P3: partition the data accordingly prior to conducting the classifications
L278@P3: step. We have evaluated the methodology by using the AVIRIS
L279@P3: instrument. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed
L280@P3: strategy can exploit the information contained in each spectrometer
L281@P3: in order to improve the classification results using limited training
L282@P3: samples. In the future, we will use other imaging spectrometers
L283@P3: and classification techniques in order to analyze the generality of
L284@P3: the presented approach. We are also planning on using different
L285@P3: numbers of bands for each partition (in the present configuration all
L286@P3: partitions have the same number of bands) in order to better model
L287@P3: the contributions from each spectrometer.
